Chapter 22

A Kit 3 app from nothing

Kit 2's svelte.config.js and $lib are gone in Kit 3, and the tsconfig has to say which files are yours.

By the end of this chapter

Create the venue app and understand every line of its configuration.

We have a matching engine, a log, projections and a ledger. None of it has a screen. This part builds the SvelteKit 3 application that participants actually use, and it starts with configuration — not because configuration is interesting, but because Kit 3 moved four things and each one produces a confusing error if you carry a Kit 2 habit into it.

That is the whole scaffold. There is no npx sv create step in this course because typing the files out is how you find out what each one is for.

Kit 2's svelte.config.js is gone

In Kit 2, svelte.config.js held the adapter, the aliases, the CSRF setting and the compiler options, and vite.config.js held Vite's. Two files, one project, and a constant low-level question of which one a given setting lived in. Kit 3 deletes the first: everything is an option on the sveltekit() Vite plugin.

Line by line, because every one of these is load-bearing:

  • defineConfig(({ mode }) => …) — a *function*, not an object. loadEnv has to run before the plugin is constructed, because paths.origin needs a value out of .env and Vite has not read those yet when a plain object literal is evaluated. Write it as an object and PUBLIC_ORIGIN is undefined at exactly the moment it is needed.
  • paths.origin — the origin the app believes it is served from. More on this in a moment; it is the single most surprising thing in the file. The origin constant above it strips any trailing slash first, for a reason chapter 23 explains.
  • csrf.trustedOrigins — Kit 2 turned its form-submission check off with checkOrigin: false; Kit 3 removed that option, and trustedOrigins: ['*'] is how you say the same thing now. It is narrower than it looks: calls to remote functions keep a same-origin check of Kit's own that ignores this setting. We set ['*'] and write our own check, for reasons that get a whole chapter.
  • compilerOptions.runes: true — no legacy mode. Every component is runes-only, so a Svelte 4 export let left in by habit is a compile error telling you to use $props(), rather than a component that quietly runs in legacy mode.
  • compilerOptions.experimental.async: true — turns on await inside $derived and in component markup. The terminal is built on it.
  • experimental.remoteFunctions: true — turns on .remote.ts files. Forget it and every remote module fails to compile, in vite dev and in the build alike. The error does at least name the flag and give you the exact snippet to add to the sveltekit() options.
  • ssr.external — @libsql/client loads a native .node binary. Vite cannot bundle that, and the error if it tries is a module-not-found for a file that plainly exists.

Experimental means what it says

Two of those flags are called experimental because they are. SvelteKit's documentation says it plainly of remote functions — "This feature is currently experimental, meaning it is likely to contain bugs and is subject to change without notice" — and async Svelte is behind a flag for the same reason. For a production venue that is a real cost: an upgrade can change an API this app is built on, and the release notes for those two features are reading you cannot skip. The course uses them anyway, deliberately. They are where SvelteKit is going, they remove a great deal of plumbing — a typed function instead of a load function, an endpoint and a fetch — and the places they break are exactly what a course about running a real system should teach. Load functions and form actions are not legacy: they are the stable primitives, fully supported, and a team that cannot absorb a breaking change in a minor release should build on them. Chapter 24 shows what this project uses in their place.

paths.origin is baked in at build time

This is not a runtime setting. adapter-node v6 reads paths.origin during vite build and compiles the value into the output. Change your domain and you must rebuild, not restart. And when the value is absent the adapter falls back to reconstructing the origin from the Host header, assuming https — so a plain-HTTP preview computes https://localhost:4173, which never matches the real http://localhost:4173, and every single POST returns 403 with no explanation beyond "Cross-site POST form submissions are forbidden".

If a deployed Kit 3 app suddenly rejects every form and you changed nothing but the hostname, paths.origin is the first place to look — and a restart will not fix it.

Kit 2's $lib is gone too

Kit 2 generated a $lib alias for you. Kit 3 does not: it uses Node subpath imports — a plain package.json feature that existed long before Kit and needs no bundler magic to understand.

Two things changed and both catch people. The prefix is # because that is the character Node reserved for internal imports, and the file extension is required. Not .js standing in for a TypeScript file — the actual .ts. Node's type stripping resolves what you wrote, so what you write has to exist.

Why this is better than an alias

A $lib alias only exists inside the bundler. Run a file under plain node, feed it to a test runner that does not share the config, or point an editor at it without the plugin loaded, and the import is unresolvable. #lib/* is resolved by Node itself, so a script, a test, an editor and the bundler all agree without being told anything.

The tsconfig has to say which files are yours

This one cost an afternoon. You still extend a base config that svelte-kit sync generates, but two things changed. The base is now $app/tsconfig rather than Kit 2's ./.svelte-kit/tsconfig.json. And the Kit 3 base deliberately sets no include and no exclude. The first is a one-line edit. The second is where the afternoon went.

Two thousand nine hundred and fifty-two type errors, none of them in code anybody wrote. With no include, TypeScript falls back to "every file under this directory", so svelte-check walked into build/ and type-checked the app's own minified production output. The fix is to say what you meant:

.svelte-kit/types/**/*.ts must be in include. That is where Kit writes the generated route types that ./$types resolves to. Leave it out and every PageServerLoad import fails with a module-not-found for a file that is sitting right there on disk.

The list is also how the browser tests get type-checked. e2e/**/*.ts and playwright.config.ts are the end-to-end suite you meet in chapter 41; listing them means svelte-check reads them like any other file, so a test that calls a locator method that does not exist fails pnpm check rather than failing in a browser five minutes into verify.

noUncheckedIndexedAccess deserves a note. It makes array[0] have type T | undefined, which sounds pedantic until you remember what this application is. Half the code on a trading screen is "the best bid" — and on a book with nothing in it, the honest answer genuinely is "there isn't one". The flag stops us pretending otherwise.

Checkpoint

  • You can explain where Kit 3 configuration lives and why defineConfig takes a function
  • You can explain what paths.origin does and why changing it needs a rebuild
  • You can write a #lib/* import from memory, extension included
  • You know why include and exclude are not optional in a Kit 3 tsconfig
